opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest lesson was humility about how much work it takes to get one right. People see a scaling law as a clean line on a log-log plot and assume that's where you start. It's really where you end up, after a huge amount of careful, unglamorous experimentation.

That project was with Jonathan Rosenfeld, who did a lot of the heavy lifting on the functional forms, along with Mike Carbin and Nir Shavit. A few things stuck with me.

**The functional form matters a lot.** A pure power law is a nice approximation, but real error curves aren't power laws everywhere. When you prune a network you see a low-error plateau where removing weights barely matters. Then there's a power-law region where error climbs predictably as you remove more. Finally there's a high-error plateau where the network basically stops working. If you fit a straight line to only part of that, you get something that looks great in-sample and falls apart when you extrapolate. You have to think about the shape of the whole curve, including the transitions.

**You need to vary many things together.** We weren't just asking how error depends on sparsity. We were asking how it depends on sparsity, width, depth, and dataset size jointly. What surprised me was how much structure there was: you could often fold several of those dimensions into a single quantity that behaves consistently. But you only discover that by sweeping many dimensions. If you vary one knob at a time, you miss the interactions, and the interactions are where the interesting regularities live.

**The goal is prediction, not description.** Fitting a curve to points you already have isn't impressive. A good functional form will fit almost anything. The real test is whether you can fit on small, cheap configurations and accurately predict large, expensive ones you haven't run. That's the practical value: deciding what to spend compute on before you spend it. So we tried to be disciplined about holding things out and checking extrapolation, not just reporting goodness of fit.

**Your training setup has to be solid at every scale.** If hyperparameters are tuned well for small models and poorly for large ones, or the reverse, you're not measuring a scaling law. You're measuring your tuning budget. A lot of disagreement in the scaling literature traces back to this. The law is only as trustworthy as the consistency of the experiments underneath it.

**Scaling laws are empirical regularities, not physics.** They hold within the regime you measured, under the method you used. Change the pruning algorithm, the architecture family, or the data distribution, and the constants can shift, sometimes the form too. I think of them as an extremely useful engineering tool, a way to make budgeting and planning more scientific. I'm wary of treating them as fundamental truths to extrapolate many orders of magnitude out.

That mindset carried into how I think about large-scale training more broadly. Before committing serious resources to a big run, you want small, cheap experiments that tell you, with some confidence, what will happen at scale. That project taught me both how powerful that is when it works and how carefully you have to do it for it to work at all.

r001.rationale: The response says that a clean line on a log-log plot is only where the work ends, and that fitting part of the curve can look good in-sample yet fail on extrapolation. This clearly communicates that an apparent fit alone does not establish a valid scaling law.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the pruning scaling law work, that was with Jonathan Rosenfeld, Joel Veness, Nir Shavit, and Michael Carbin, and honestly the biggest lesson wasn't about pruning at all. It was about what it actually takes to say you have a scaling law.

The question we started with was pretty simple. If I take a network, train it, and then prune away some fraction of the weights, how does the error depend on how much I pruned, how big the network was, and how much data it saw? And people had tons of anecdotal results, plots for one architecture on one dataset. But a scaling law is a much stronger claim. You're saying there's a functional form that holds across orders of magnitude, with a small number of parameters, and that if I give you a few points you can predict the rest.

What I learned is that the hard part is being honest about the degrees of freedom. It is very easy to fit a curve. You can throw a power law with enough knobs at almost anything and it'll look beautiful on a log-log plot. The real test is whether the fit extrapolates. So we got religious about holding out the large models and the heavy pruning regimes, fitting only on the small cheap stuff, and asking whether we could predict the expensive points we hadn't shown the model. If the answer is no, you don't have a law, you have a summary of your data.

The second thing was that the interesting structure lives in how variables interact. The naive thing is to treat density, width, depth, and data as independent and multiply some terms together. That doesn't work. What we found was that there's basically a low-error regime where pruning is nearly free, then a transition, then a high-error regime where it falls apart, and the location of that transition moves as a function of the other variables. Getting that joint behavior right, rather than fitting each axis separately, was most of the work. And I think that generalizes. The scaling laws people get wrong are usually the ones where they measured along one axis and assumed it factorized.

And the third lesson, which is maybe the uncomfortable one, is that a scaling law is a statement about a procedure, not about neural networks in the abstract. We were pruning with iterative magnitude pruning and retraining in a specific way. Change the pruning algorithm, change the training recipe, and the constants move. Sometimes the shape moves. So I came out of it much more cautious about anyone, including me, saying "the scaling law for X." You have to say the scaling law for X under this exact recipe, in this regime, and here's how far I've actually verified it extrapolates. Most of what gets called a scaling law in this field is a nice fit to the region someone could afford to run, and the places where it would break are precisely the places nobody has looked yet.

r001.rationale: The response says a curve can look beautiful on a log-log plot, but that the real test is whether it extrapolates; without that, it is only a summary of the data.

astra-6.text:
The biggest lesson was that getting a scaling law right is much harder than finding a curve that fits your data. With pruning, you’re varying the size of the original network, how much you prune it, and how much data you train on. A relationship can look very convincing in one slice of that space and fall apart when you look somewhere else.

So you have to be systematic about the experiments and pay attention to where the proposed law fails. Does it capture the transitions between different regimes? Does it predict experiments you didn’t use to fit it? And are you measuring a property of the networks, or a property of your particular training and pruning procedure?

That made me much more cautious about extrapolation. A good fit is a starting point. The more interesting test is whether the law makes a prediction you can go out and try to break.

r001.rationale: The response says that finding a curve that fits the data is not enough to establish a scaling law, and calls for testing its predictions beyond the fitted experiments. This communicates the criterion’s core point, though it does not mention a log-log plot explicitly.

sol-6.1.text:
The biggest lesson was that getting a nice-looking power law is the easy part. Figuring out what you have to measure, and whether that relationship actually predicts something you haven’t measured yet, is much harder.

With pruning, there are a bunch of variables interacting: the size of the network you start with, how much you prune it, how much data you have, and how you train it. If you only look at one slice of that space, you can convince yourself you’ve found a very general relationship when you’ve really found something that holds in a fairly narrow regime.

So you need experiments that can distinguish between different explanations, rather than just more points along the same curve. And you want to hold out experiments—ideally at scales you didn’t fit on—and ask whether your law predicts them. Otherwise, you’ve got a description of your results, which can be useful, but it’s not necessarily a tool for making decisions.

That made me much more appreciative of how much careful empirical work goes into a good scaling law. The simple equation at the end hides a lot of work figuring out where it applies and where it breaks.

r001.rationale: The response says a nice-looking power law is insufficient: it may hold only in a narrow regime, so held-out experiments must test whether it predicts unmeasured results.
